questions.question: What is async/await in JavaScript and how does it work?
questions.title: Async Await Basics
questions.direct_answer: async marks a function as returning a Promise. await pauses the async function (NOT the thread) until the Promise resolves. It's syntax over Promises — the same mechanics, sequential-looking code.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[async fn] -->|await| P[suspend fn — not thread]
    P -->|resolve| R[resume with value]
    A →|return| W[wraps in Promise]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The compiler-level view (the depth interviewers probe): an async function is a state machine — each await is a suspension point. The function's code is split at each await into states; the engine's regenerator/async-to-generator transform compiles them into a step function that the Promise resolution drives. The observable behavior: the function runs to the first await, returns a pending Promise, and the continuation (after the await) runs as the awaited Promise's resolution callback — a microtask.

The sequential default's cost (the interview's practical test): await in a for-loop is sequential by construction — each iteration's fetch starts only when the previous finishes. The parallel patterns: Promise.all for independent same-shape calls, Promise.allSettled when partial failures are acceptable, and the batched loop for (const chunk of chunks) for controlled parallelism.

The top-level await (the modern addition): in ES modules, await works at the top level (no async wrapper) — the module itself loads asynchronously. The cost: modules that import it wait for its resolution — the dependency-tree blocking to understand when someone asks 'why does my module load slowly?'
